chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter I
paragraphs: [Speaking in French] "Well, Prince, so Genoa and Lucca are now nothing more than estates belonging to the Bonaparte family. But I'm warning you — if you don't tell me this means war, if you keep on defending the atrocities committed by that Antichrist — and I truly believe he is the Antichrist — then I'm done with you. You are no longer my friend, no longer my 'faithful slave,' as you like to call yourself! But how are you? I can see I've frightened you — sit down and tell me all the news."

It was July 1805, and the speaker was the well-known Anna Pavlovna Scherer, lady-in-waiting and favorite of the Empress Marya Fedorovna. These were the words with which she greeted Prince Vasili Kuragin, a man of high rank and influence, who was the first to arrive at her reception. Anna Pavlovna had been coughing for several days. She was suffering from la grippe, as she put it — grippe being a fashionable new word in St. Petersburg at the time, used only by the elite.
All of her invitations, without exception written in French, had been delivered that morning by a footman in scarlet livery. They all read the same way:

[Speaking in French] "If you have nothing better to do, Count (or Prince), and if the prospect of spending an evening with a poor invalid isn't too terrible, I would be delighted to see you tonight between seven and ten. — Annette Scherer."

"Good heavens! What a fierce attack!" replied the prince, not at all put out by this reception. He had just walked in wearing an embroidered court uniform with knee breeches and buckled shoes, decorations glinting on his chest, his flat face wearing a look of calm self-assurance. He spoke in that refined French in which an earlier generation not only conversed but thought, and with the gentle, patronizing tone that comes naturally to a man of importance who has grown old in the ways of society and the court. He walked up to Anna Pavlovna, kissed her hand, offered her a view of his bald, perfumed, gleaming head, and settled himself comfortably on the sofa.

[Speaking in French] "First of all, dear friend, tell me how you are. Put your friend's mind at rest," he said, his tone unchanged — beneath the politeness and the show of sympathy, one could detect indifference, even irony.

"How can anyone be well when they're suffering morally? How can anyone stay calm in times like these, if they have any feeling at all?" said Anna Pavlovna. "You are staying the whole evening, I hope?"
"And the party at the English ambassador's? Today is Wednesday. I need to put in an appearance there," said the prince. "My daughter is coming to pick me up."
"I thought today's event had been canceled. I must say, all these celebrations and fireworks are becoming tiresome."
"If they had known you wished it, the entertainment would have been postponed," said the prince, who, like a wound-up clock, said things out of habit that he didn't even expect to be believed.
"Don't tease! Well, and what has been decided about Novosiltsev's dispatch? You know everything."

"What can one say about it?" replied the prince in a cold, indifferent tone. "What has been decided? They've decided that Bonaparte has burned his bridges, and I believe we are prepared to burn ours."

Prince Vasili always spoke in a languid drawl, like an actor going through a stale role. Anna Pavlovna, on the other hand, despite her forty years, overflowed with energy and passion. Being an enthusiast had become her social calling, and sometimes, even when she didn't feel like it, she would work herself into a state of enthusiasm so as not to disappoint the people who expected it of her. The faint smile that always played around her lips — though it didn't really suit her faded features — expressed, like a spoiled child's, a constant awareness of her charming weakness, which she neither wished, nor could, nor saw any reason to correct.
In the middle of a conversation about politics, Anna Pavlovna burst out:

"Oh, don't speak to me about Austria! Perhaps I don't understand these things, but Austria has never wanted war and doesn't want it now. She is betraying us! Russia alone must save Europe. Our gracious sovereign understands his sacred duty and will remain true to it. That is the one thing I believe in! Our good and noble sovereign must fulfill the highest role on earth, and he is so virtuous and noble that God will not abandon him. He will fulfill his calling and crush the monster of revolution, which has become more terrible than ever in the person of this murderer and villain! We alone must avenge the blood of the righteous. Who else can we count on? England, with her commercial mentality, will never understand Emperor Alexander's nobility of soul. She has refused to leave Malta. She looks for hidden motives behind everything we do. What answer did Novosiltsev get? None. The English have not understood, and cannot understand, the selflessness of our Emperor, who seeks nothing for himself but only the good of humanity. And what have they promised? Nothing! And the little they have promised, they won't deliver! Prussia has always insisted that Bonaparte is invincible and that all of Europe is powerless against him. And I don't believe a word Hardenberg says, or Haugwitz either. This famous Prussian neutrality is nothing but a trap. I have faith only in God and in the noble destiny of our beloved sovereign. He will save Europe!"
She broke off suddenly, smiling at her own intensity.

"I think," said the prince with a smile, "that if you had been sent instead of our dear Wintzingerode, you would have taken the King of Prussia's consent by storm. You are so eloquent. Will you give me a cup of tea?"

[Speaking in French] "In a moment. By the way," she added, growing calm again, "I'm expecting two very interesting men tonight: the Vicomte de Mortemart, who is connected to the Montmorencys through the Rohans — one of the finest French families. He is one of the true émigrés, the genuine ones. And also the Abbé Morio. Do you know that brilliant thinker? He has been received by the Emperor. Had you heard?"

"I shall be delighted to meet them," said the prince. "But tell me," he added with studied casualness, as though the thought had only just occurred to him — though the question he was about to ask was the real reason for his visit — "is it true that the Dowager Empress wants Baron Funke appointed as first secretary at Vienna? From what I hear, the baron is a rather mediocre fellow."
Prince Vasili wanted this post for his own son, but others were trying, through the Dowager Empress Marya Fedorovna, to secure it for the baron.
Anna Pavlovna half-closed her eyes, as if to indicate that neither she nor anyone else had any right to question what the Empress desired or approved of.
"Baron Funke has been recommended to the Dowager Empress by her sister," was all she said, in a dry, sorrowful tone.

As she mentioned the Empress, Anna Pavlovna's face suddenly took on an expression of deep and genuine devotion and respect, mixed with sadness — and this happened every time she spoke of her illustrious patroness. She added that Her Majesty had been gracious enough to show Baron Funke a great deal of esteem, and her face clouded over with sadness once more.

The prince said nothing and looked unconcerned. But with the womanly quickness and social instinct that came naturally to her, Anna Pavlovna wanted both to reproach him — for daring to speak that way about someone recommended by the Empress — and at the same time to console him, so she said:
"Now about your family. Do you know that since your daughter came out in society, everyone has been captivated by her? They say she is astonishingly beautiful."
The prince bowed to express his respect and gratitude.

"I often think," she continued after a short pause, moving closer to the prince and smiling warmly, as if to signal that politics and social topics were finished and it was time for personal conversation — "I often think how unfairly the joys of life are sometimes distributed. Why has fate given you two such wonderful children? I'm not talking about Anatole, your youngest. I don't like him," she added in a tone that left no room for argument, raising her eyebrows. "Two such charming children. And yet you appreciate them less than anyone, which means you don't deserve them."
And she flashed her rapturous smile.
"I can't help it," said the prince. "Lavater would have said I lack the bump of fatherly feeling."

"Don't joke. I mean to have a serious talk with you. Do you know I'm unhappy with your younger son? Between ourselves" — and her face took on its melancholy expression — "he was mentioned at Her Majesty's court, and you were pitied..."
The prince said nothing, but she looked at him meaningfully, waiting for a reply. He frowned.

"What would you have me do?" he said at last. "You know I did everything a father could for their education, and they've both turned out to be fools. Hippolyte is at least a quiet fool, but Anatole is an active one. That's the only difference between them." He said this with a smile more natural and animated than usual, so that the lines around his mouth clearly revealed something unexpectedly coarse and unpleasant.
"And why are children born to men like you? If you weren't a father, there would be nothing I could reproach you with," said Anna Pavlovna, looking up thoughtfully.
"I am your faithful slave, and to you alone can I confess that my children are the curse of my existence. It is the cross I have to bear. That's how I explain it to myself. What can be done?"
He said no more, but conveyed his resignation to a cruel fate with a gesture. Anna Pavlovna reflected for a moment.

"Have you ever thought of marrying off your wayward son Anatole?" she asked. "They say old maids have a passion for matchmaking, and though I don't feel that weakness in myself just yet, I do know a young woman who is very unhappy with her father. She's a relation of yours — Princess Marya Bolkonskaya."
Prince Vasili did not reply, but with the quick memory and social perception of a man of the world, he gave a slight nod of the head to show he was considering the idea.

"Do you know," he said at last, clearly unable to hold back the gloomy current of his thoughts, "that Anatole is costing me forty thousand rubles a year? And," he went on after a pause, "what will it be in five years if he carries on like this?" After a moment he added, "That's what we fathers have to deal with. Is this princess of yours wealthy?"

"Her father is very rich and very miserly. He lives in the country. He's the famous Prince Bolkonski who had to retire from the army under the last Emperor and was nicknamed 'the King of Prussia.' He's very clever but eccentric, and a bore. The poor girl is very unhappy. She has a brother — I think you know him — he recently married Lise Meinen. He's an aide-de-camp to Kutuzov and will be here tonight."

"Listen, dear Annette," said the prince, suddenly taking Anna Pavlovna's hand and for some reason pulling it downward. "Arrange that match for me and I shall be your most devoted slave forever — 'slave' with an f, as one of my village elders writes in his reports. She is rich and from a good family, and that's all I need."

And with the easy, familiar grace that was so natural to him, he raised the lady-in-waiting's hand to his lips, kissed it, and swung it gently back and forth as he leaned back in his armchair, looking off in another direction.

[Speaking in French] "Wait," said Anna Pavlovna, thinking it over. "I'll speak to Lise — young Bolkonski's wife — this very evening, and perhaps the thing can be arranged. It will be on your family's behalf that I begin my apprenticeship as an old maid."

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter II
paragraphs: Anna Pavlovna's drawing room was gradually filling up. The highest society of Petersburg was gathered there: people who differed widely in age and temperament but who all belonged to the same social world. Prince Vasili's daughter, the beautiful Hélène, came to collect her father for the ambassador's party; she wore a ball gown and her badge as lady-in-waiting. The youthful little Princess Bolkonskaya, known as the most captivating woman in Petersburg, was also there. She had married the previous winter and, being pregnant, no longer attended large gatherings — only small receptions. Prince Vasili's son Hippolyte had arrived with Mortemart, whom he introduced. The Abbé Morio and many others had come as well.
* The most fascinating woman in Petersburg.

To each new guest Anna Pavlovna said, "You haven't yet seen my aunt," or "You don't know my aunt?" — and with great solemnity she escorted each one over to a little old lady wearing large ribbon bows in her cap, who had come sailing in from another room as soon as the guests began arriving. Slowly turning her eyes from the visitor to her aunt, Anna Pavlovna would announce each person's name and then leave them.

Every guest went through the ritual of greeting this old aunt whom none of them knew, none of them wanted to know, and none of them cared about. Anna Pavlovna watched these greetings with mournful, solemn interest and silent approval. The aunt said the same thing to each of them: she asked about their health and spoke of her own, and about the health of Her Majesty, who "thank God, was feeling better today." And each guest, though politeness prevented them from showing impatience, left the old woman with a sense of relief at having performed an annoying obligation, and did not go near her again for the rest of the evening.

The young Princess Bolkonskaya had brought some needlework in a gold-embroidered velvet bag. Her pretty little upper lip, on which a faint dark down was just visible, was too short for her teeth, but this only made it curl up more sweetly, and was especially charming when she sometimes drew it down to meet her lower lip. As is always the case with a truly attractive woman, her flaw — the shortness of her upper lip and her half-open mouth — seemed to be her own unique and special form of beauty. Everyone brightened at the sight of this pretty young woman, so soon to be a mother, so full of life and health, carrying her burden so lightly. Old men and bored, dispirited young ones who spent time in her company and talked with her felt as though they too were becoming, like her, full of life and energy. Everyone who spoke with her, watching at each word her bright smile and the constant gleam of her white teeth, thought themselves to be in an especially good mood that day.

The little princess circled the table with quick, short, swaying steps, her workbag on her arm, and cheerfully spreading out her skirts, sat down on a sofa near the silver samovar as though everything she did was a pleasure to herself and to everyone around her. [Speaking in French] "I've brought my work," she said, showing her bag and addressing the whole room. [Speaking in French] "Mind you, Annette, I hope you haven't played a trick on me," she added, turning to her hostess. [Speaking in French] "You wrote that it would be just a small gathering — and look how badly I'm dressed." And she spread her arms wide to show off her short-waisted, lace-trimmed, elegant gray dress, cinched with a broad ribbon just below the bust.
[Speaking in French] "Don't worry, Lise — you will always be prettier than anyone else," replied Anna Pavlovna.

[Speaking in French] "You know," said the princess in the same tone of voice, still in French, turning to a general, "my husband is abandoning me? He's going off to get himself killed. Tell me — what is this awful war even for?" she added, turning to Prince Vasili, and without waiting for an answer she turned to speak to his daughter, the beautiful Hélène.
"What a delightful woman this little princess is!" said Prince Vasili to Anna Pavlovna.

One of the next guests to arrive was a heavyset young man with close-cropped hair, spectacles, and the light-colored trousers that were fashionable at the time. He wore a very high collar ruffle and a brown dress coat. This stout young man was the illegitimate son of Count Bezukhov, a well-known grandee from Catherine the Great's era, who was now lying on his deathbed in Moscow. The young man had not yet entered either the military or the civil service, having only just returned from abroad where he had been educated; this was his first appearance in society. Anna Pavlovna greeted him with the minimal nod she reserved for the lowest tier of her drawing room hierarchy. But despite this cold welcome, a look of anxiety and alarm crossed her face when she saw Pierre enter — as though something too large and unsuited to the room had appeared. And although he was certainly bigger than the other men present, her unease could only have stemmed from the clever yet shy, observant yet natural expression that set him apart from everyone else in that drawing room.
[Speaking in French] "It is so good of you, Monsieur Pierre, to come visit a poor invalid," said Anna Pavlovna, exchanging an anxious look with her aunt as she led him over.
Pierre mumbled something inaudible and kept looking around as though searching for something. On his way to the aunt, he smiled warmly at the little princess, as one does to a close acquaintance.

Anna Pavlovna's alarm proved justified, for Pierre turned away from the aunt without waiting to hear her remarks about Her Majesty's health. Anna Pavlovna caught him in dismay and said, "Do you know the Abbé Morio? He is a most interesting man."
"Yes, I've heard about his plan for perpetual peace, and it's very interesting — but hardly practical."

"You think so?" said Anna Pavlovna, wanting to say something before escaping to attend to her duties as hostess. But Pierre now committed a second social blunder. First he had walked away from a lady before she finished speaking to him; now he continued talking to someone who clearly wanted to get away. With his head bent forward and his big feet planted wide apart, he launched into an explanation of why he considered the abbé's plan unrealistic.
"We'll discuss it later," said Anna Pavlovna with a smile.

Having rid herself of this young man who didn't know how to behave, she went back to her duties as hostess, continuing to observe and listen, ready to step in wherever the conversation might stall. Like the foreman in a spinning mill who, after setting the workers to their tasks, walks around noticing where a spindle has stopped or where one is creaking or making too much noise, and hurries to slow it down or get it running properly — so Anna Pavlovna moved through her drawing room, approaching first a group that had gone quiet, then one that had grown too loud, and with a word here or a slight adjustment there, she kept the conversational machine running smoothly and steadily. But through all of this, her anxiety about Pierre was obvious. She watched nervously whenever he drifted near the group around Mortemart to listen in, and again when he moved on to the circle gathered around the abbé.

Pierre had been educated abroad, and this evening at Anna Pavlovna's was the first society reception he had attended in Russia. He knew that all the intellectual stars of Petersburg were gathered here, and like a child in a toy shop, he didn't know which way to look, afraid of missing some brilliant conversation. Seeing the self-assured, polished expressions on the faces around him, he kept expecting to hear something truly profound. At last he made his way over to Morio. The conversation there seemed interesting, and he stood waiting for a chance to share his own views, the way young people always do.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter III
paragraphs: Anna Pavlovna's reception was in full swing. The spindles hummed steadily and ceaselessly on all sides. Aside from the aunt — beside whom sat only one elderly lady whose thin, careworn face seemed rather out of place in this brilliant company — the entire gathering had arranged itself into three groups. One, mostly male, had formed around the abbé. Another, made up of younger people, clustered around the beautiful Princess Hélène, Prince Vasili's daughter, and the little Princess Bolkonskaya, who was very pretty and rosy-cheeked, though perhaps a bit plump for her age. The third group was gathered around Mortemart and Anna Pavlovna.

The vicomte was a good-looking young man with soft features and polished manners, who clearly considered himself a celebrity but was modest enough, out of politeness, to make himself available to whatever circle he found himself in. Anna Pavlovna was clearly serving him up as a treat for her guests. Just as a skilled chef presents as a rare delicacy a cut of meat that no one who had seen it in the kitchen would have wanted to eat, Anna Pavlovna offered up first the vicomte and then the abbé as especially choice morsels. The group around Mortemart immediately began discussing the murder of the Duc d'Enghien. The vicomte said that the duc had perished because of his own noble nature, and that Bonaparte had particular reasons for hating him.
[Speaking in French] "Ah, yes! Do tell us all about it, Vicomte," said Anna Pavlovna, pleased that the phrase had a certain Louis XV ring to it: [Speaking in French] "Tell us the story, Vicomte."
The vicomte bowed and smiled graciously to show his willingness to oblige. Anna Pavlovna arranged a group around him, inviting everyone to listen to his story.

"The vicomte knew the duc personally," Anna Pavlovna whispered to one guest. "The vicomte is a marvelous storyteller," she told another. "You can tell at once he belongs to the very best society," she said to a third. And so the vicomte was served up to the company in the finest possible style, like a beautifully garnished roast on a silver platter.
The vicomte was about to begin his story and gave a subtle smile.
"Come here, Hélène dear," said Anna Pavlovna to the beautiful young princess who was sitting some distance away, at the center of another group.

The princess smiled. She rose with the same unchanging smile she had worn since entering the room — the smile of a flawlessly beautiful woman. With a light rustle of her white dress trimmed with moss and ivy, with a gleam of white shoulders, glossy hair, and sparkling diamonds, she passed between the men who stepped aside for her. She looked at none of them, yet smiled at all of them, as though graciously granting each one the privilege of admiring her beautiful figure and shapely shoulders, back, and bosom — which, as was the fashion, were very much on display — and she seemed to bring the glamour of a ballroom with her as she crossed toward Anna Pavlovna. Hélène was so stunning that she showed not the slightest trace of flirtation; on the contrary, she almost seemed embarrassed by her own overwhelming beauty. She appeared to wish, but to be unable, to lessen its effect.

"How lovely!" said everyone who saw her; and the vicomte lifted his shoulders and lowered his eyes as if startled by something extraordinary when she took her seat across from him and turned her unchanging smile upon him as well.
[Speaking in French] "Madame, I doubt my abilities before such an audience," he said, smiling and inclining his head.

The princess rested her bare, rounded arm on a small table and evidently felt no reply was needed. She waited with a smile. Throughout the story she sat upright, glancing now at her beautiful round arm, its shape slightly altered where it pressed against the table, now at her still more beautiful bosom, where she adjusted a diamond necklace. From time to time she smoothed the folds of her dress, and whenever the story produced a particular effect, she glanced at Anna Pavlovna, instantly adopted the same expression she saw on the hostess's face, and then settled back into her radiant smile.
The little princess had also left the tea table and followed Hélène.
"Wait a moment — let me get my work. Now then, what are you thinking about?" she said, turning to Prince Hippolyte. "Fetch me my workbag."
There was a general stir as the princess, smiling and chatting merrily with everyone at once, sat down and cheerfully arranged herself in her seat.
"Now I'm all settled," she said, and asking the vicomte to begin, she picked up her needlework.
Prince Hippolyte brought over the workbag, then joined the circle and pulled a chair up close to hers, seating himself beside her.

The charming Hippolyte was remarkable for his extraordinary resemblance to his beautiful sister, but even more remarkable for the fact that, despite this resemblance, he was strikingly ugly. His features were like his sister's, but while in her case everything was illuminated by a joyous, self-satisfied, youthful, ever-present smile and by the wonderful classical beauty of her figure, his face was dulled by a look of imbecility and an expression of sullen self-importance, while his body was thin and weak. His eyes, nose, and mouth all seemed scrunched into a vacant, weary grimace, and his arms and legs always settled into unnatural positions.
"This isn't going to be a ghost story, is it?" he said, sitting down beside the princess and hastily adjusting his eyeglass, as though he couldn't begin to speak without this instrument.
"Why no, my dear fellow," said the astonished storyteller, shrugging his shoulders.
"Because I hate ghost stories," said Prince Hippolyte in a tone that suggested he only understood the meaning of his own words after he had said them.

He spoke with such self-assurance that his listeners could never be quite sure whether what he said was very witty or very stupid. He was dressed in a dark green coat and knee breeches the color of what he himself called "startled nymph's thigh," with shoes and silk stockings.

The vicomte told his story very neatly. It was an anecdote making the rounds at the time, about how the Duc d'Enghien had secretly gone to Paris to visit Mademoiselle George; that at her house he had come upon Bonaparte, who also enjoyed the famous actress's favors; and that in the duc's presence, Napoleon happened to fall into one of the fainting spells he was prone to, leaving him entirely at the duc's mercy. The duc spared him — and this act of mercy Bonaparte later repaid with execution.
The story was very pretty and engaging, especially the part where the rivals suddenly recognized each other, and the ladies looked moved.
"Charming!" said Anna Pavlovna, glancing inquiringly at the little princess.
"Charming!" whispered the little princess, pushing her needle into her embroidery as if to prove that the story was so fascinating it prevented her from continuing her work.

The vicomte appreciated this silent praise and, smiling gratefully, prepared to go on. But just then Anna Pavlovna, who had been keeping a watchful eye on the young man who made her so nervous, noticed that Pierre was talking too loudly and too intensely with the abbé, and hurried over to intervene. Pierre had managed to start a conversation with the abbé about the balance of power, and the abbé, clearly drawn in by the young man's earnest enthusiasm, was laying out his favorite theory. Both were talking and listening with too much natural eagerness — which was exactly what Anna Pavlovna disapproved of.

"The means are the balance of power in Europe and the rights of the people," the abbé was saying. "All that's needed is for one powerful nation like Russia — however barbaric she may be called — to place herself unselfishly at the head of an alliance dedicated to maintaining the European balance of power, and the world would be saved!"
"But how do you actually achieve that balance?" Pierre began.

At that moment Anna Pavlovna appeared and, looking sternly at Pierre, asked the Italian how he was finding the Russian climate. The Italian's face changed instantly, taking on an offensively affected, sugary expression — clearly his habitual manner when speaking with women.

[Speaking in French] "I am so enchanted by the brilliance of the wit and culture in this society — especially the feminine society — in which I have had the honor of being received, that I have not yet had time to think about the climate," he said.
Keeping both the abbé and Pierre from escaping, Anna Pavlovna brought them into the larger circle, the better to keep them under observation.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter IV
paragraphs: Just then another guest entered the drawing room: Prince Andrei Bolkonski, the little princess's husband. He was a very handsome young man of medium height, with firm, sharply defined features. Everything about him — from his weary, bored expression to his quiet, measured stride — stood in the sharpest contrast to his lively little wife. It was clear that he not only knew everyone in the room but found them all so tiresome that it exhausted him to look at or listen to them. And of all the faces he found so tedious, none seemed to bore him quite as much as his pretty wife's. He turned away from her with a grimace that marred his handsome face, kissed Anna Pavlovna's hand, and squinting slightly, surveyed the entire company.
"You are off to the war, Prince?" said Anna Pavlovna.

[Speaking in French] "General Kutuzov" — said Bolkonski, speaking French and stressing the last syllable of the general's name in the French manner — "has been kind enough to take me on as an aide-de-camp..."
"And Lise, your wife?"
"She will go to the country."
"Aren't you ashamed to deprive us of your charming wife?"

[Speaking in French] "André," said his wife, addressing her husband in the same flirtatious way she spoke to other men, "the vicomte has been telling us the most wonderful story about Mademoiselle George and Bonaparte!"

Prince Andrei screwed up his eyes and looked away. Pierre, who had been watching him with glad, affectionate eyes from the moment he entered the room, now came up and took his arm. Before Prince Andrei could even look around, he frowned again — annoyed at whoever was touching his arm — but when he saw Pierre's beaming face, he broke into an unexpectedly warm and genuine smile.
"Well, well! So you've made it into high society too?" he said to Pierre.
"I knew you would be here," replied Pierre. "I'll come to supper with you. May I?" he added in a low voice, so as not to disturb the vicomte, who was still telling his story.

"No, impossible!" said Prince Andrei, laughing and squeezing Pierre's hand to show that there was no need to ask. He wanted to say something more, but just then Prince Vasili and his daughter stood up to leave, and the two young men rose to let them pass.

[Speaking in French] "You must excuse me, dear Vicomte," said Prince Vasili to the Frenchman, holding him by the sleeve in a friendly way to keep him from getting up. "This wretched party at the ambassador's is robbing me of a pleasure and forcing me to cut you short. I'm truly sorry to leave your delightful gathering," he said, turning to Anna Pavlovna.

His daughter, Princess Hélène, passed between the chairs, lightly gathering up the folds of her gown, her smile shining even more brilliantly on her beautiful face. Pierre gazed at her with fascinated, almost frightened eyes as she swept past him.
"Very lovely," said Prince Andrei.
"Very," said Pierre.

As he passed, Prince Vasili seized Pierre's hand and said to Anna Pavlovna, "Educate this bear for me! He's been staying at my house for a whole month and this is the first time I've seen him out in society. Nothing is as essential for a young man as the company of intelligent women."

Anna Pavlovna smiled and promised to take Pierre in hand. She knew his father was connected to Prince Vasili. The elderly lady who had been sitting with the old aunt rose quickly and hurried after Prince Vasili into the entrance hall. All the artificial interest she had been showing dropped away from her kind, careworn face, which now expressed nothing but anxiety and fear.
"What about my son Boris, Prince?" she said, following him into the hall. "I can't stay in Petersburg any longer. Tell me — what news can I bring back to my poor boy?"

Although Prince Vasili listened reluctantly and rather rudely to the elderly lady, even showing signs of impatience, she gave him a fawning, pleading smile and seized his hand to prevent him from leaving.
"What would it cost you to put in a word with the Emperor? Then he would be transferred to the Guards immediately," she said.

"Believe me, Princess, I'm prepared to do everything I can," answered Prince Vasili, "but it's difficult for me to petition the Emperor. I'd advise you to go through Prince Golitsyn to Rumyantsev. That would be the best approach."

The elderly lady was Princess Drubetskaya, from one of the finest families in Russia, but she was poor and had been out of society for so long that she had lost all her old connections. She had come to Petersburg for the sole purpose of securing a position in the Guards for her only son. In fact, it was specifically to see Prince Vasili that she had obtained an invitation to Anna Pavlovna's reception and had sat through the vicomte's story. Prince Vasili's words alarmed her; a bitter expression clouded her once-handsome face — but only for a moment. Then she smiled again and gripped Prince Vasili's arm even more tightly.

"Listen to me, Prince," she said. "I have never asked you for anything, and I never will again. I have never reminded you of my father's friendship with you. But now I beg you, for God's sake, do this for my son — and I shall always consider you my benefactor," she added quickly. "No, don't be angry — just promise me! I've already asked Golitsyn and he refused. Be the kindhearted man you have always been," she said, trying to smile though tears stood in her eyes.
[Speaking in French] "Papa, we're going to be late," said Princess Hélène, turning her beautiful head and glancing back over her sculpted shoulder as she waited by the door.

Social influence, however, is a form of capital that must be spent carefully if it is to last. Prince Vasili understood this, and having realized that if he used his influence on behalf of everyone who came asking, he would soon have none left for himself, he had become cautious about spending it. But in Princess Drubetskaya's case, after her second appeal, he felt something close to a pang of conscience. She had reminded him of something that was perfectly true: he owed his first steps in his career to her father. Moreover, he could see from her manner that she was one of those women — mostly mothers — who, once they have set their minds on something, will not rest until they get what they want, and are fully prepared to keep insisting day after day, hour after hour, and if necessary, to make scenes. This last thought moved him.

[Speaking in French] "My dear Anna Mikhaylovna," he said with his usual familiar, weary tone, "it's nearly impossible for me to do what you're asking. But to prove my devotion to you and my respect for your father's memory, I will do the impossible. Your son will be transferred to the Guards. Here is my hand on it. Are you satisfied?"
"My dear benefactor! This is what I expected from you — I knew your kindness!" He turned to go.

"Wait — just one more thing! When he's been transferred to the Guards..." She hesitated. "You're on good terms with Mikhail Ilarionovich Kutuzov... recommend Boris to him as an adjutant! Then I'll be at peace, and then..."
Prince Vasili smiled.

"No, that I can't promise. You have no idea how Kutuzov is being hounded since his appointment as Commander-in-Chief. He told me himself that every lady in Moscow has conspired to foist her son on him as an adjutant."
"No, but do promise! I won't let you go! My dear benefactor..."
[Speaking in French] "Papa," said his beautiful daughter in the same tone as before, "we're going to be late."
[Speaking in French] "Well, goodbye then! Goodbye! You hear her?"
"So tomorrow you'll speak to the Emperor?"
"Yes, definitely. But about Kutuzov — that I don't promise."

[Speaking in French] "Do promise, do promise, Vasili!" cried Anna Mikhaylovna as he left, wearing the smile of a flirtatious girl — which had probably once come naturally to her but was now very poorly suited to her careworn face.

She seemed to have forgotten her age, and out of long habit was employing all her old feminine wiles. But the moment the prince was gone, her face resumed its former cold, artificial expression. She went back to the group where the vicomte was still holding forth, and once again pretended to listen while she waited for the right moment to leave. Her mission was accomplished.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter V
paragraphs: "And what do you make of this latest farce — the coronation in Milan?" asked Anna Pavlovna. "And the comedy of the people of Genoa and Lucca presenting their petitions to Monsieur Bonaparte, while Monsieur Bonaparte sits on a throne and graciously grants the wishes of nations? It's beyond belief! It's enough to make your head spin! It's as if the whole world has gone mad."
Prince Andrei looked Anna Pavlovna straight in the face with a sardonic smile.
[Speaking in French] "'God has given it to me — let anyone who touches it beware!'" he said, then repeated the words in Italian: [Speaking in Italian] "'Dio mi l'ha dato. Guai a chi la tocchi!'"
* God has given it to me, let him who touches it beware!
"I hope this will be the last straw," Anna Pavlovna continued. "The sovereigns will not be able to tolerate this man who threatens everything."

[Speaking in French] "The sovereigns? I'm not speaking of Russia," said the vicomte, politely but without hope. "The sovereigns, madame — what have they done for Louis XVII, for the Queen, for Madame Elizabeth? Nothing!" He grew more animated. "And believe me, they are reaping what they sowed when they betrayed the Bourbon cause. The sovereigns! They're sending ambassadors to congratulate the usurper."
He sighed disdainfully and shifted his position again.

Prince Hippolyte, who had been staring at the vicomte through his eyeglass for some time, suddenly turned his whole body toward the little princess and, asking her for a needle, began tracing the Condé coat of arms on the table. He explained it to her with as much gravity as if she had asked him to do it.
[Speaking in French] "A red baton, engrailed, on an azure field — the house of Condé," he said.
The princess listened with a smile.

"If Bonaparte remains on the throne of France for another year," the vicomte continued, with the air of a man who, being better informed than anyone else on the subject, doesn't listen to others but follows his own train of thought, "things will have gone too far. Through intrigue, violence, exile, and executions, French society — I mean good French society — will have been destroyed forever, and then..."
He shrugged his shoulders and spread his hands. Pierre wanted to say something — the conversation interested him — but Anna Pavlovna, who had been watching him, cut in first.

"Emperor Alexander," she said, with the melancholy that always accompanied any mention she made of the imperial family, "has declared that he will leave it to the French people to choose their own form of government. And I believe that once they are free of the usurper, the entire nation will throw itself into the arms of its rightful king," she concluded, trying to be gracious toward the royalist émigré.
"That's doubtful," said Prince Andrei. "The vicomte is quite right in saying that things have already gone too far. I think it will be very difficult to go back to the old order."
"From what I've heard," said Pierre, blushing as he broke into the conversation, "almost the entire aristocracy has already gone over to Bonaparte's side."
"That's what the Bonapartists say," replied the vicomte, without looking at Pierre. "At the present time it's hard to know the true state of French public opinion."
"Bonaparte himself has said so," remarked Prince Andrei with a sarcastic smile.
It was clear that he didn't like the vicomte and was directing his remarks at him, even while avoiding his gaze.

"'I showed them the path to glory, but they did not follow it,'" Prince Andrei continued after a brief silence, again quoting Napoleon's words. "'I opened my antechambers and they came crowding in.' I don't know how far he was justified in saying that."

"Not in the least," replied the vicomte. "After the murder of the duc, even his most devoted admirers stopped calling him a hero. If to some people," he went on, turning to Anna Pavlovna, "he ever was a hero, after the murder of the duc there was one more martyr in heaven and one fewer hero on earth."

Before Anna Pavlovna and the others could smile their appreciation of this neat line, Pierre broke into the conversation again, and though Anna Pavlovna was certain he would say something inappropriate, she was unable to stop him.

"The execution of the Duc d'Enghien," declared Pierre, "was a political necessity, and it seems to me that Napoleon showed greatness of soul by taking the full responsibility for that act upon himself."
[Speaking in French] "God! My God!" murmured Anna Pavlovna in a horrified whisper.
"What, Monsieur Pierre — you think assassination shows greatness of soul?" said the little princess, smiling and pulling her embroidery closer.
"Oh! Oh!" exclaimed several voices.
"Capital!" said Prince Hippolyte in English, and began slapping his knee with his palm.
The vicomte merely shrugged his shoulders. Pierre looked solemnly at his audience over his spectacles and continued.

"I say this," he went on with growing intensity, "because the Bourbons fled from the Revolution and abandoned the people to chaos. Napoleon alone understood the Revolution and brought it under control, and so, for the general good, he could not stop short on account of one man's life."
"Won't you come over to the other table?" suggested Anna Pavlovna.
But Pierre went on without paying her any attention.

"No," he cried, growing more and more passionate, "Napoleon is great because he rose above the Revolution, stamped out its worst excesses, and preserved everything good in it — equality before the law, freedom of speech, freedom of the press — and that is the only reason he gained power."
"Yes — if, having gained power, he had restored it to the rightful king instead of using it to commit murder, then I would call him a great man," remarked the vicomte.

"He couldn't do that. The people gave him power so that he could rid them of the Bourbons, and because they recognized that he was a great man. The Revolution was a magnificent thing!" declared Pierre, betraying by this reckless and provocative statement his extreme youth and his eagerness to say everything that was on his mind.
"What? Revolution and regicide — a magnificent thing? Well, after that... But won't you come to the other table?" Anna Pavlovna repeated.
[Speaking in French] "Rousseau's Social Contract," said the vicomte with a condescending smile.
"I'm not talking about regicide. I'm talking about ideas."
"Yes — ideas of robbery, murder, and regicide," someone interjected in an ironic voice.
"Those were extremes, certainly, but they aren't the main point. What matters are the rights of man, the liberation from prejudice, equality before the law — and Napoleon has upheld all of these."

"Liberty and equality," said the vicomte with contempt, as though finally deciding to demonstrate to this young man how foolish his words were. "Grand phrases that have long been discredited. Who doesn't love liberty and equality? Even our Savior preached liberty and equality. Have people become happier since the Revolution? On the contrary. We wanted freedom, and Bonaparte has destroyed it."

Prince Andrei watched with an amused smile, looking from Pierre to the vicomte and from the vicomte to their hostess. In the first moment of Pierre's outburst, Anna Pavlovna had been horrified, despite all her social experience. But when she saw that Pierre's blasphemous words had not outraged the vicomte, and had satisfied herself that it was impossible to shut Pierre up, she rallied her forces and joined the vicomte in a vigorous counterattack on the young orator.

[Speaking in French] "But my dear Monsieur Pierre," she said, "how do you explain the fact that a great man would execute a duke — or even an ordinary person — who is innocent and has not been tried?"
"I would like to ask," said the vicomte, "how monsieur explains the 18th Brumaire. Was that not a fraud? It was a swindle, pure and simple — nothing like the behavior of a great man!"
"And the prisoners he killed in Africa! That was horrible!" said the little princess, shrugging her shoulders.
"He's a despicable man, no matter what anyone says," remarked Prince Hippolyte.

Pierre, not knowing whom to answer, looked around at all of them and smiled. His smile was unlike the half-smiles of other people. When he smiled, his serious, even somewhat gloomy expression was instantly replaced by something else — a childlike, kind, even slightly foolish look that seemed to ask forgiveness.
The vicomte, who was meeting Pierre for the first time, saw clearly that this young radical was not nearly as dangerous as his words suggested. Everyone fell silent.

"How do you expect him to answer all of you at once?" said Prince Andrei. "Besides, when judging a statesman, you have to distinguish between his actions as a private individual, as a general, and as an emperor. At least that's how it seems to me."
"Yes, yes — exactly!" Pierre chimed in, delighted at this reinforcement.

"One must admit," Prince Andrei continued, "that Napoleon the man was great on the bridge at Arcola, and in the hospital at Jaffa where he clasped the hands of plague victims. But... there are other actions that are hard to justify."
Prince Andrei, who had clearly been trying to soften the awkwardness of Pierre's remarks, stood up and signaled to his wife that it was time to go.
Suddenly Prince Hippolyte jumped up, gestured for everyone's attention, and asked them all to sit down, then began:

"I was told the most charming Moscow story today, and I simply must share it with you. Excuse me, Vicomte — I have to tell it in Russian or the whole point will be lost." And Prince Hippolyte launched into his story in the kind of Russian a Frenchman would speak after about a year in Russia. Everyone waited, so insistently did he demand their attention.

"There is a lady in Moscow — une dame — and she is very stingy. She insists on having two footmen behind her carriage, and very big ones. That's what she likes. And she had a maid, also big. She said..."
Here Prince Hippolyte paused, visibly struggling to recall his thoughts.
"She said... Oh yes! She said, 'Girl' — to the maid — 'put on a livery, get up behind the carriage, and come with me while I make some calls.'"
Here Prince Hippolyte sputtered and burst out laughing long before his audience, which did not help the story. A few people, including the elderly lady and Anna Pavlovna, did manage a smile.

"She went. Suddenly there was a great gust of wind. The girl lost her hat and her long hair came tumbling down..." Here he could barely get the words out through his gasps of laughter: "And the whole world found out..."

And so the story ended. Although it was impossible to say why he had told it, or why it had to be told in Russian, still, Anna Pavlovna and the others appreciated Prince Hippolyte's social instinct in so neatly defusing Pierre's uncomfortable and graceless outburst. After the anecdote, the conversation dissolved into harmless small talk about the latest ball and the next one, about the theater, and about who would see whom, and when and where.
